intro: Paediatric emergencies covers the seriously ill or injured child: recognition and resuscitation, airway and breathing emergencies, anaphylaxis, seizures, dehydration and DKA, surgical emergencies, poisoning and injury. The AMC tests these heavily because they are life-threatening, time-critical and depend on weight-based doses and Australian guidance (ANZCOR, RCH Melbourne, ASCIA, Poisons Information Centre).

lessons.title: The seriously ill child and resuscitation
objectives: Recognise the seriously ill child using a rapid ABCDE assessment and age-appropriate vital signs
Run paediatric basic and advanced life support using the ANZCOR DRSABCD approach
Estimate weight and calculate the key resuscitation doses (adrenaline, fluid bolus, glucose, defibrillation)
Start early management of paediatric septic shock and drowning

sections.heading: Why children are different
sections.body:
Children rarely arrest from a primary cardiac cause. The usual pathway is **respiratory failure or shock leading to hypoxia, then bradycardia, then asystole**. That is why paediatric resuscitation puts so much weight on airway and breathing, and why a **bradycardic child is a peri-arrest child**.

Children also compensate well and then fall off a cliff. Blood pressure is maintained until late, so **hypotension is a pre-terminal sign** in a child. Tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, cool peripheries and altered behaviour come first.

In Australia the leading causes of death in children aged 1 to 4 are injury (drowning prominent among them), congenital conditions and cancer. Drowning in backyard pools, bathtubs and dams is a recurring AMC theme, which is why **pool fencing is legislated** (details vary by state) and "active supervision" is the public health message. Resuscitation in Australia follows **ANZCOR** (Australian and New Zealand Committee on Resuscitation) guidelines, and paediatric emergency care commonly follows the **RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines**.

sections.heading: Rapid assessment: the first minute
sections.body:
Use a quick "doorway" look, then **ABCDE**.

- **Appearance**: tone, interaction, consolability, look/gaze, speech/cry. A floppy, quiet, disinterested child is worrying; a screaming child at least has an airway and perfusion.
- **Work of breathing**: recession, tracheal tug, head bobbing, nasal flaring, grunting (a sign of severe distress in infants), stridor or wheeze.
- **Circulation to skin**: pallor, mottling, cyanosis. Central capillary refill over 2 seconds is abnormal.

Approximate normal vital signs (use your local observation chart, which in Australia usually has age-banded colour zones and an escalation response):

| Age | Heart rate (/min) | Resp rate (/min) |
|---|---|---|
| Under 1 year | 110-160 | 30-40 |
| 1-2 years | 100-150 | 25-35 |
| 2-5 years | 95-140 | 25-30 |
| 5-12 years | 80-120 | 20-25 |
| Over 12 years | 60-100 | 15-20 |

**D** includes AVPU or GCS, pupils, posture and a **bedside glucose** ("don't ever forget glucose"). **E** includes temperature, rash (non-blanching?), injuries that don't fit the story.

Most Australian hospitals use paediatric early warning tools linked to rapid response (for example NSW "Between the Flags"). The AMC expects you to escalate early rather than watch a deteriorating child.

sections.heading: Basic and advanced life support (ANZCOR)
sections.body:
**DRSABCD**: Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing, CPR, Defibrillation.

- **Airway**: head tilt-chin lift. In **infants keep the head neutral** (their large occiput already flexes the neck); in older children use a "sniffing" position.
- **Breathing**: if not breathing normally, give **2 initial breaths**. Agonal gasps are not normal breathing.
- **Compressions**: lower half of the sternum, **depth about one third of the chest's AP diameter**, rate **100-120/min**. Infants: two fingers, or two thumbs with hands encircling the chest when there are two rescuers.
- **Ratio**: **30:2** for lay rescuers and single rescuers; ANZCOR supports **15:2** for two trained healthcare rescuers in children.

**Advanced life support**

- Attach monitor/defibrillator early. Most paediatric arrests are **non-shockable (asystole or PEA)**.
- **Adrenaline 10 microg/kg** (0.1 mL/kg of 1:10 000) IV or IO, then every second 2-minute cycle (about every 4 minutes). In non-shockable rhythms give it as soon as access is obtained.
- **Shockable (VF/pulseless VT): 4 J/kg**, resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes, then reassess. Adrenaline after the second shock; amiodarone 5 mg/kg after the third.
- **IO access** if IV is not obtained quickly (proximal tibia is the usual site).
- Look for reversible causes: the **4 Hs and 4 Ts** (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia and metabolic including hypoglycaemia, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis).

**Weight and doses**. Use a measured or parent-reported weight where possible. The traditional formula for ages 1-10, **(age + 4) x 2 kg**, is a rough guide; newer APLS formulae or length-based tapes are also used.

| Intervention | Dose |
|---|---|
| Fluid bolus | 10-20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride, reassess after each |
| Hypoglycaemia | 2 mL/kg 10% glucose |
| Adrenaline (arrest) | 10 microg/kg IV/IO |
| Defibrillation | 4 J/kg |

sections.heading: Septic shock and drowning
sections.body:
**Paediatric sepsis** kills through delay. Suspect it in a febrile (or hypothermic) child with tachycardia, altered mental state, poor perfusion or a non-blanching rash. Australian state sepsis pathways (for example the NSW and Queensland paediatric sepsis pathways) emphasise:

1. High-flow oxygen, IV or IO access, **blood culture, glucose, lactate/blood gas**.
2. **Empirical IV antibiotics within 1 hour** of recognition (commonly a third-generation cephalosporin, with additions depending on age and source: check eTG and local guidelines; young infants need cover for Listeria and group B strep).
3. **Fluid bolus 10-20 mL/kg** of isotonic crystalloid, reassess, repeat; after about 40-60 mL/kg without response, think inotropes and call retrieval/PICU.
4. Treat hypoglycaemia; consider meningitis (lumbar puncture only once stable).

**Drowning** is hypoxic arrest. Priorities are **oxygenation and ventilation**: start with breaths, then standard CPR. Cervical spine injury is uncommon unless there was diving or a high-impact mechanism. Vomiting is common during resuscitation: turn the child to the side and clear the airway. All children who needed resuscitation, or who have ongoing cough, breathlessness, hypoxia or reduced consciousness, need hospital assessment, because deterioration from aspiration pneumonitis can be delayed by several hours.

Prevention is part of the answer: four-sided isolation pool fencing with self-closing gates, active adult supervision within arm's reach for toddlers, and parental CPR training.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- "Most important next step" in an unresponsive child: open the airway and give breaths before worrying about IV access.
- A child with bradycardia and poor perfusion despite oxygenation needs **CPR if HR is under 60/min**.
- The dose questions are straightforward if you remember the four numbers: **10 microg/kg, 10-20 mL/kg, 2 mL/kg 10% glucose, 4 J/kg**.
- Hypotension in a child means decompensated shock: the right answer is urgent fluid and escalation, not "repeat obs in 30 minutes".
- For a drowned toddler who looks well now, the trap is discharging immediately: observe for delayed respiratory deterioration.
- Always check glucose in any child with altered consciousness or seizure.

keyPoints: Paediatric arrest is usually hypoxic; airway and breathing come first.
Hypotension is a late, pre-terminal sign of shock in children.
CPR: depth one third of chest, 100-120/min; 30:2 lay, 15:2 two healthcare rescuers.
Adrenaline 10 microg/kg IV/IO; defibrillation 4 J/kg; fluid bolus 10-20 mL/kg; 10% glucose 2 mL/kg.
Most paediatric arrest rhythms are non-shockable.
Sepsis: cultures, IV antibiotics within 1 hour, reassess after each bolus.
Drowning: prioritise ventilation; observe for delayed deterioration.
redFlags: Bradycardia in a sick child (peri-arrest)
Hypotension (decompensated shock)
Grunting, silent chest or exhaustion
Reduced conscious level or floppy infant
Non-blanching rash with fever
Capillary refill over 3 seconds with mottled skin

contrast.india: Often taught from AHA/IAP PALS algorithms.
contrast.australia: ANZCOR guidelines, taught as DRSABCD; RCH Melbourne CPGs widely used for paediatric doses.

contrast.india: Open water and wells; little regulation of home water hazards.
contrast.australia: Backyard pools dominate; pool fencing is law (varies by state) and active supervision is the key message.

flashcards.front: Adrenaline dose in paediatric cardiac arrest?
flashcards.back: 10 microg/kg IV/IO (0.1 mL/kg of 1:10 000), every second cycle (about every 4 minutes).

flashcards.front: Defibrillation energy for a child in VF?
flashcards.back: 4 J/kg.

flashcards.front: Treatment of hypoglycaemia in a sick child?
flashcards.back: 10% glucose 2 mL/kg IV/IO, then recheck.

flashcards.front: Heart rate threshold to start CPR in an infant with poor perfusion?
flashcards.back: Under 60/min despite adequate oxygenation and ventilation.

flashcards.front: Compression depth in paediatric CPR?
flashcards.back: About one third of the anteroposterior chest diameter.

flashcards.front: Initial fluid bolus in paediatric shock?
flashcards.back: 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid, reassess after each bolus.

quiz.stem: A 3-year-old boy (about 14 kg) is pulled from a backyard pool by his father after an unknown time submerged. In the emergency department he is unresponsive and not breathing, and no pulse is felt. The monitor shows asystole. Two nurses and you are present, IO access has just been placed and bag-valve-mask ventilation with oxygen is underway. What is the most appropriate drug and dose to give now?
options: Adrenaline 140 microg IO
Adrenaline 1.4 mg IO
Amiodarone 70 mg IO
Atropine 280 microg IO
Sodium bicarbonate 14 mmol IO
quiz.explanation:
In paediatric arrest the adrenaline dose is **10 microg/kg** IV or IO, which for 14 kg is 140 microg (1.4 mL of 1:10 000). In **non-shockable rhythms** (asystole, PEA), adrenaline is given as soon as vascular access is available, alongside high-quality CPR, then every second 2-minute cycle.

Drowning causes a hypoxic arrest, so effective ventilation with oxygen is just as important as the drug. Amiodarone belongs to shockable rhythms after the third shock. Atropine is not part of arrest algorithms, and bicarbonate is not routine.

**Rule:** asystole in a child = CPR, ventilation, adrenaline 10 microg/kg now.
whyWrong: This is ten times the correct dose (a classic 1:1000 vs 1:10 000 error).
Amiodarone is for shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT, not asystole.
Atropine is not used in cardiac arrest algorithms.
Bicarbonate is not routine and does not replace adrenaline and ventilation.
quiz.ausPearl: Drowning is a leading cause of death in Australian toddlers; four-sided pool fencing is legislated, with details varying by state.

quiz.stem: A 2-year-old girl presents with 1 day of fever and lethargy. She is drowsy but rousable. HR 180/min, RR 44/min, BP 85/50 mmHg, temperature 39.6 °C, central capillary refill 4 seconds, cool mottled legs. There are a few non-blanching spots on her legs. IV access is obtained. Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Lumbar puncture, then antibiotics once CSF results are available
Oral paracetamol and reassess in one hour
Maintenance IV fluids and CT head
Blood culture, IV ceftriaxone and a 10-20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus
Admit to the ward for 4-hourly observations
quiz.explanation:
Fever, a non-blanching rash and signs of shock (tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, mottling, altered conscious state) are **meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise**. Her BP is preserved, which is typical of compensated shock in children: do not be reassured by it.

Immediate steps: oxygen, **blood culture (without delaying treatment), IV third-generation cephalosporin within the first hour**, and a **fluid bolus of 10-20 mL/kg** isotonic crystalloid with reassessment after each. Check glucose and a gas. Lumbar puncture is **contraindicated** in a shocked, drowsy child and must never delay antibiotics.

**Rule:** sick, febrile child with shock = antibiotics and fluid now; investigations that delay treatment are wrong.
whyWrong: LP is unsafe in shock and reduced consciousness and would delay antibiotics.
This child is in septic shock; antipyretics and waiting are dangerous.
She needs a resuscitation bolus, not maintenance fluid, and CT does not change immediate care.
Ward observations ignore established shock; she needs resuscitation and likely PICU review.
quiz.ausPearl: Invasive meningococcal disease is notifiable in all states; public health arranges clearance antibiotics for close contacts.

quiz.stem: A 7-month-old boy is brought in with bronchiolitis that has worsened over 3 days. He was grunting and tiring on arrival. Despite high-flow oxygen by mask his SpO2 is 82%, and his heart rate has fallen from 170/min to 55/min. He is now floppy and pale. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give atropine 20 microg/kg IV
Give a 20 mL/kg fluid bolus
Start bag-valve-mask ventilation with 100% oxygen and begin chest compressions if the heart rate stays under 60/min
Arrange an urgent chest X-ray
Attach defibrillator pads and deliver 4 J/kg
quiz.explanation:
In children, **bradycardia is usually hypoxic**. This infant has progressed from respiratory distress to exhaustion, hypoxia and now bradycardia, the step just before arrest. The treatment of hypoxic bradycardia is **oxygenation and ventilation**: open the airway (neutral position in an infant) and give bag-valve-mask ventilation with 100% oxygen. If the heart rate stays **under 60/min with poor perfusion** despite adequate ventilation, **start chest compressions** and follow the arrest algorithm.

Atropine only has a role in vagally mediated bradycardia (for example during intubation). Fluids, X-rays and defibrillation all miss the underlying problem.
whyWrong: Atropine does not fix hypoxic bradycardia; oxygenation does.
He is not primarily hypovolaemic; the problem is failed breathing.
Imaging delays the life-saving intervention.
Sinus bradycardia is not a shockable rhythm.

lessons.title: Airway and breathing emergencies
objectives: Manage the choking child using the ANZCOR back blow and chest thrust sequence
Recognise inhaled foreign body and know that a normal chest X-ray does not exclude it
Distinguish severe croup, epiglottitis and bacterial tracheitis and manage each safely
Grade acute asthma severity and start first-line treatment in the emergency department

sections.heading: Why the paediatric airway obstructs easily
sections.body:
A child's airway is narrow, so a little oedema causes a big fall in radius and a much bigger rise in resistance (resistance rises roughly with the fourth power of the fall in radius). Toddlers explore by mouth, have immature molars and a poor cough, so **peak age for inhaled foreign body is 1-3 years**. Nuts, grapes, popcorn and small toy parts are classic culprits.

Stridor means upper airway (extrathoracic) narrowing; wheeze means lower airway narrowing. A **quiet child with a severe obstruction is more worrying than a noisy one**: soft stridor and reduced air entry can mean exhaustion.

The AMC usually tests four scenarios: the choking toddler, the sub-acute inhaled foreign body, the child with stridor and fever (croup vs epiglottitis vs tracheitis), and the child with acute severe asthma. (Routine croup and bronchiolitis are covered under paediatric infections.)

sections.heading: Choking and inhaled foreign body
sections.body:
**Choking first aid (ANZCOR)**

- **Effective cough** (crying, talking, coughing forcefully): encourage coughing, stay with the child, call for help if it does not resolve. Do not slap the back of a child who is coughing well.
- **Ineffective cough, conscious**: call 000, give **up to 5 back blows** (infant prone, head down, along the forearm/thigh), then **up to 5 chest thrusts**, checking after each whether the obstruction has cleared. Alternate. ANZCOR recommends chest thrusts rather than abdominal thrusts.
- **Unconscious**: start CPR. Look in the mouth before breaths and remove a visible object; **no blind finger sweeps**.

**Inhaled foreign body (sub-acute)**

Classic history: sudden choking or coughing episode while eating or playing, which settles, followed by persistent cough, **unilateral wheeze** or reduced air entry, or recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe. The episode may not have been witnessed, so ask.

Investigations:
- **Chest X-ray** (inspiratory and expiratory, or lateral decubitus films in toddlers): most foreign bodies (nuts) are radiolucent. Look for **unilateral hyperinflation from air trapping** (ball-valve effect: the affected side stays inflated on expiration and the mediastinum shifts away), or collapse/consolidation distal to the object.
- **A normal chest X-ray does not exclude it.**

Management: **rigid bronchoscopy** under general anaesthetic when history is suggestive, even with a normal film.

sections.heading: Stridor with fever: croup, epiglottitis, tracheitis
sections.body:
| Feature | Croup | Epiglottitis | Bacterial tracheitis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Age | 6 months-3 years | Classically 2-7 years (now rare) | Any, often after viral croup |
| Cause | Parainfluenza and other viruses | Hib (rare since vaccine), strep, staph | Staph aureus, strep |
| Onset | Coryza, then barking cough, worse at night | Hours; very unwell | Croup that suddenly worsens |
| Cough | **Barking** | Usually absent | Present, harsh |
| Look | Usually not toxic | **Toxic, drooling, sitting forward (tripod), soft muffled voice**, cannot swallow | Toxic, high fever |

**Severe croup**: stridor at rest, marked recession, agitation or lethargy, hypoxia. Give **nebulised adrenaline** (RCH uses 0.5 mL/kg of 1:1000, maximum 5 mL) plus a corticosteroid (oral **dexamethasone 0.15-0.3 mg/kg** or prednisolone), observe for several hours afterwards because the adrenaline effect wears off, and involve senior/anaesthetic help if it is not responding. Keep the child calm on the parent's lap.

**Suspected epiglottitis**: **do not examine the throat, lie the child down, or upset them** (for example cannulating or X-raying) because this can precipitate complete obstruction. Call the most senior anaesthetist and ENT, secure the airway in theatre, then give IV antibiotics (third-generation cephalosporin) after cultures. Close contacts of Hib disease may need rifampicin prophylaxis (public health advice).

**Bacterial tracheitis**: suspect when a child with "croup" becomes toxic and does not respond to adrenaline; often needs intubation and IV antibiotics.

sections.heading: Acute asthma in the emergency department
sections.body:
Assess severity using the whole picture; do not rely on a single sign. Australian guidance (National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook, RCH CPG) groups children roughly as:

| Severity | Features |
|---|---|
| Mild/moderate | Can talk in sentences, mild or moderate work of breathing, alert |
| Severe | Can say only words, marked recession, agitation, SpO2 below about 92% |
| Life-threatening | **Silent chest, cyanosis, drowsiness or exhaustion, unable to speak**, poor respiratory effort |

**Treatment**
- **Salbutamol by pMDI and spacer**: 6 puffs for age 1-5, 12 puffs for age 6 and over, repeated as needed (every 20 minutes in the first hour for moderate-severe). Spacers work as well as nebulisers in most children; nebulise with oxygen if life-threatening or if hypoxic and unable to use a spacer.
- **Oxygen** to keep SpO2 in the target range (usually 92-95%).
- **Oral prednisolone** about 1 mg/kg daily (check RCH/AAH for maximum and duration) for moderate to severe attacks.
- **Ipratropium** added in the first hour for severe or life-threatening asthma.
- Escalation: IV magnesium sulfate, IV salbutamol or aminophylline, non-invasive ventilation, PICU. Life-threatening asthma needs senior help immediately.

**Discharge**: stable on 3-hourly or less frequent salbutamol, a written **asthma action plan**, spacer technique checked, preventer reviewed, GP follow-up within a few days.

sections.heading: Traps and discriminating clues
sections.body:
- **Unilateral wheeze in a toddler = foreign body until proven otherwise**, even without a witnessed choking episode. Normal X-ray does not change the answer: bronchoscopy.
- Drooling, sitting forward, no cough, toxic: epiglottitis. The correct answer is "call senior anaesthetist and ENT", and the wrong answers are "examine the throat with a tongue depressor" and "lateral neck X-ray".
- Croup that stops responding and becomes toxic: bacterial tracheitis.
- A silent chest in asthma is not improvement; it is life-threatening.
- Choking with an effective cough: encourage coughing, do not intervene.
- Spacer over nebuliser for most children with acute asthma.

keyPoints: Choking: effective cough, encourage; ineffective cough, 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts; unconscious, CPR.
No blind finger sweeps.
Inhaled foreign body: sudden choking then unilateral wheeze; rigid bronchoscopy even if the X-ray is normal.
Expiratory film shows unilateral air trapping with mediastinal shift away from the affected side.
Epiglottitis: drooling, toxic, tripod, no barking cough; do not examine the throat; senior airway help.
Severe croup: nebulised adrenaline plus dexamethasone, then observe.
Acute asthma: salbutamol via spacer (6 puffs under 6, 12 puffs 6 and over), oral prednisolone, ipratropium if severe.
redFlags: Stridor at rest or soft stridor with exhaustion
Drooling and inability to swallow
Silent chest, cyanosis or drowsiness in asthma
Toxic child with croup not responding to adrenaline
Ineffective cough in a choking child

contrast.india: Heimlich (abdominal thrusts) commonly taught for children.
contrast.australia: ANZCOR: back blows then chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts are not recommended.
pMDI with spacer is first-line for most children; nebulise if life-threatening.

flashcards.front: First action for a choking toddler who cannot cough effectively but is conscious?
flashcards.back: Call 000; up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 chest thrusts, alternating.

flashcards.front: Radiological sign of an inhaled foreign body on expiratory film?
flashcards.back: Unilateral hyperinflation (air trapping) with mediastinal shift away from the affected side.

flashcards.front: Definitive management of suspected inhaled foreign body?
flashcards.back: Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia.

flashcards.front: Salbutamol dose via spacer for a 4-year-old with acute asthma?
flashcards.back: 6 puffs (12 puffs if 6 years or older).

flashcards.front: Nebulised adrenaline dose for severe croup (RCH)?
flashcards.back: 0.5 mL/kg of 1:1000, maximum 5 mL.

quiz.stem: A 20-month-old boy has had a cough for 10 days. His mother recalls he coughed and went red while eating mixed nuts at a family barbecue, but he seemed fine afterwards. He is afebrile, SpO2 96% in room air, and there is reduced air entry with wheeze over the right lung only. An inspiratory chest X-ray is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Trial of inhaled salbutamol via spacer and review in 48 hours
Oral amoxicillin for 5 days
Reassure, as the chest X-ray is normal
Arrange a sweat chloride test
Refer for urgent rigid bronchoscopy
quiz.explanation:
A witnessed **choking episode followed by persistent cough and unilateral wheeze** in a toddler is an **inhaled foreign body** until proven otherwise. Nuts are radiolucent, so the X-ray is often normal; an expiratory or decubitus film may show air trapping, but a normal film does not exclude it.

The diagnostic and therapeutic procedure is **rigid bronchoscopy** under general anaesthetic. Delay risks obstructive pneumonia, bronchiectasis and, with nuts, a marked inflammatory reaction.

**Discriminating clue:** unilateral signs. Asthma and viral wheeze are bilateral.
whyWrong: Treating as asthma delays removal; unilateral wheeze is not asthma.
There is no infection yet, and antibiotics will not remove the object.
A normal X-ray does not exclude a radiolucent foreign body.
Cystic fibrosis does not cause sudden-onset unilateral signs after choking.

quiz.stem: A 4-year-old girl who recently arrived from overseas with an incomplete immunisation history presents with 6 hours of high fever. She is sitting upright leaning forward, drooling, with a soft inspiratory stridor and a muffled voice. She has no cough. Temperature 39.9 °C, HR 160/min, SpO2 94% on room air. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Examine the pharynx with a tongue depressor to look at the epiglottis
Keep her calm with her parent, give oxygen as tolerated, and call the senior anaesthetist and ENT surgeon
Insert an IV cannula and take blood cultures before anything else
Arrange a lateral soft-tissue neck X-ray
Give oral dexamethasone and discharge with croup advice
quiz.explanation:
Toxic appearance, drooling, tripod posture, muffled voice and **absence of a barking cough** point to **acute epiglottitis**. It is rare since Hib vaccination, which is why the incomplete immunisation history is the discriminating clue.

Anything that distresses the child (examining the throat, cannulation, lying her flat, sending her to radiology) can precipitate **complete airway obstruction**. Keep her calm upright on the parent, give oxygen if tolerated, and summon the most experienced anaesthetist and ENT surgeon to secure the airway in theatre. Cultures and IV antibiotics (third-generation cephalosporin) follow once the airway is safe.
whyWrong: Examining the throat can precipitate complete obstruction.
Cannulation distresses the child; do it once the airway is secured.
Leaving the resuscitation area for X-ray is dangerous and delays airway control.
This is not croup; she is toxic with no barking cough.

quiz.stem: A 7-year-old boy with known asthma is brought to the emergency department with 1 day of worsening wheeze. He can only say single words, has marked subcostal recession and is agitated. RR 40/min, HR 140/min, SpO2 90% in room air. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Oxygen and salbutamol 12 puffs via spacer, repeated every 20 minutes, plus ipratropium and oral prednisolone
IV aminophylline infusion
Oral montelukast and review in 1 hour
Salbutamol 2 puffs without a spacer
Nebulised budesonide alone
quiz.explanation:
Speaking in words, marked recession, agitation and SpO2 under about 92% indicate **severe acute asthma**. First-line treatment is **oxygen** to target saturations, **frequent salbutamol** (12 puffs via spacer for a child 6 or older, or nebulised if unable to use a spacer or life-threatening), **ipratropium** added in the first hour for severe attacks, and **oral prednisolone**.

IV agents (magnesium, salbutamol, aminophylline) are escalation for children not responding. Montelukast and inhaled corticosteroids are preventers and do nothing for an acute severe attack.
whyWrong: Aminophylline is a later escalation step, not first-line.
Montelukast is a preventer, not acute treatment.
Inadequate dose, and a spacer is needed for effective delivery.
Inhaled steroids alone do not relieve acute bronchospasm.
quiz.ausPearl: The National Asthma Council's Australian Asthma Handbook is the reference for asthma dosing and action plans.

lessons.title: Anaphylaxis in children
objectives: Diagnose anaphylaxis using ASCIA criteria, including presentations without skin signs
Give the correct IM adrenaline dose and choose the right autoinjector for a child's weight
Manage refractory anaphylaxis and know the observation period after treatment
Arrange discharge with an ASCIA action plan, autoinjector training and allergist referral

sections.heading: What anaphylaxis is and why Australia takes it seriously
sections.body:
Anaphylaxis is a **severe, potentially life-threatening systemic allergic reaction**. Australia has one of the highest rates of childhood food allergy in the world: about 1 in 10 infants in Melbourne's HealthNuts study had a challenge-proven food allergy. Common triggers in children are **peanut, tree nuts, egg, cow's milk, sesame, fish and shellfish**; insect stings (bees, jack jumper ants in Tasmania and south-east Australia) and medicines matter too, especially in older children.

Because of this, schools and childcare centres in Australia hold **ASCIA action plans**, staff are trained in autoinjector use, and many schools keep a general-use autoinjector. The Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy (**ASCIA**) sets the national guidance.

sections.heading: Mechanism
sections.body:
In IgE-mediated anaphylaxis, allergen cross-links specific IgE on **mast cells and basophils**, which degranulate and release histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes and prostaglandins. These cause:

- **Vasodilation and capillary leak**: hypotension, distributive shock (up to a third of circulating volume can shift out of vessels).
- **Smooth muscle contraction**: bronchospasm, abdominal cramps, vomiting.
- **Mucosal oedema**: lip, tongue and laryngeal swelling.

**Adrenaline** reverses all three: alpha-1 vasoconstriction (raises BP, reduces oedema), beta-1 inotropy, beta-2 bronchodilation, and it stabilises mast cells. Antihistamines only block one mediator and act too slowly, which is why they are not a treatment for anaphylaxis.

Risk factors for severe or fatal reactions: **asthma (especially poorly controlled)**, adolescence (risk-taking, delayed adrenaline), peanut/tree nut allergy, and delay in giving adrenaline.

sections.heading: Recognition (ASCIA)
sections.body:
Anaphylaxis is likely when there is an **acute onset illness (minutes to hours) with skin or mucosal features (urticaria, flushing, lip swelling) plus involvement of the respiratory or cardiovascular system, or severe gastrointestinal symptoms**. It can also be diagnosed **without skin features**: acute hypotension, bronchospasm or upper airway obstruction after exposure to a known or likely allergen.

Features that mean anaphylaxis (on the ASCIA action plan):

- Difficult or noisy breathing, wheeze or persistent cough
- Swelling of the tongue, swelling or tightness in the throat
- Difficulty talking or hoarse voice
- Persistent dizziness or collapse
- **Pale and floppy (young children)**
- Abdominal pain and vomiting are signs of anaphylaxis **for insect allergy**

Hives, facial swelling or tingling mouth alone is a **mild to moderate allergic reaction**: give a non-sedating antihistamine and watch closely for progression.

Differentials are covered next.

sections.heading: What else it could be
sections.body:
| Condition | How it differs from anaphylaxis |
|---|---|
| **Vasovagal syncope** | Pallor, sweating, nausea, **bradycardia**; no urticaria, wheeze or stridor; recovers within a minute or two when lying flat. Common with injections, including vaccination |
| **Acute asthma alone** | Wheeze without skin, cardiovascular or GI features and without a clear allergen trigger. But a food-allergic child with sudden wheeze after eating has anaphylaxis until proven otherwise |
| **Generalised urticaria/angioedema alone** | Skin and lips only, no airway, breathing or circulatory involvement: mild to moderate allergic reaction (antihistamine, observe) |
| **Hereditary angioedema** | Swelling without urticaria or itch, recurrent, family history; does not respond to adrenaline well; bradykinin-mediated |
| **Septic shock** | Fever, gradual onset, no allergen exposure |
| **Panic or hyperventilation** | Paraesthesiae, normal BP and saturations, no urticaria |
| **Breath-holding spell** | Clear emotional trigger, rapid recovery |
| **Inhaled foreign body** | Choking while eating, then cough or unilateral wheeze, without skin features |

The practical rule: **if in doubt, give adrenaline**. IM adrenaline at the correct dose is very safe in children, while delay is the commonest factor in fatal anaphylaxis. Vaccination clinics in Australia keep adrenaline on hand and observe children for 15 minutes after vaccines for this reason, and staff must be able to tell a faint from anaphylaxis.

Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) is another mimic in infants: repetitive profuse vomiting 1-4 hours after a trigger food (often cow's milk, rice or egg), pallor and lethargy, with no skin or respiratory features. It is not IgE-mediated and is treated with fluids (ondansetron may help), not adrenaline.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.body:
**Immediately**

1. **Remove the allergen** if possible (flick out a bee sting).
2. **Lay the child flat**; do not let them stand or walk (sudden upright posture has caused fatal cardiovascular collapse). If breathing is difficult, allow them to sit with legs outstretched. Hold infants horizontally, not upright.
3. **IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh**: **0.01 mg/kg** of 1:1000 (0.01 mL/kg), maximum 0.5 mg. Autoinjectors: **150 microg for 7.5-20 kg, 300 microg for over 20 kg**.
4. Call 000 / call for help, give oxygen and start CPR if needed.
5. **Repeat adrenaline every 5 minutes** if no response.
6. Give asthma reliever **after** adrenaline if wheezy.

**In hospital**
- IV access, **fluid bolus 20 mL/kg** 0.9% sodium chloride for hypotension.
- Persistent or worsening after 2-3 IM doses: **adrenaline infusion** under senior guidance, with specialist/PICU involvement.
- **Mast cell tryptase** (ideally within 1-2 hours of onset and again later) helps confirm the diagnosis afterwards.
- Corticosteroids and antihistamines are adjuncts only. Avoid sedating antihistamines (promethazine), which can cause hypotension and mask drowsiness.

**Observation**: at least **4 hours** after the last adrenaline dose (ASCIA), longer (often overnight) for severe reactions, needing more than one dose, asthma, or presentation at night, because biphasic reactions occur.

**Discharge checklist**
- Prescribe an adrenaline autoinjector (PBS-subsidised) and train the family.
- Provide an **ASCIA action plan for anaphylaxis** (red plan) and a copy for school or childcare.
- Refer to a **clinical immunology/allergy specialist**.
- Optimise asthma control.
- Allergen avoidance education, and a medical alert device for older children.

sections.heading: How the AMC tests anaphylaxis
sections.body:
- The answer is almost always **IM adrenaline into the lateral thigh**, now. Not IV (outside cardiac arrest or monitored infusion), not subcutaneous, not antihistamine first.
- Check the dose arithmetic: 0.01 mg/kg = **0.01 mL/kg of 1:1000**. An 18 kg child: 0.18 mg, or a 150 microg autoinjector.
- Autoinjector weights: **7.5-20 kg = 150 microg; over 20 kg = 300 microg**.
- "Pale and floppy" in a toddler after eating = anaphylaxis, even without hives.
- The child who looks better after adrenaline still needs **4 hours of observation**.
- Asthma is the biggest risk factor for fatal food anaphylaxis.

keyPoints: Anaphylaxis: skin/mucosal features plus respiratory, cardiovascular or severe GI involvement; skin signs may be absent.
IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg (0.01 mL/kg of 1:1000), max 0.5 mg, anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5 minutes.
Autoinjector: 150 microg for 7.5-20 kg, 300 microg for over 20 kg.
Lay flat; do not stand or walk the child.
Antihistamines and steroids are not first-line.
Observe at least 4 hours after the last adrenaline dose.
Discharge with autoinjector, ASCIA action plan and allergist referral.
redFlags: Hoarse voice, throat tightness or stridor
Wheeze or persistent cough after allergen exposure
Pale and floppy young child
Hypotension or collapse
Poorly controlled asthma in a food-allergic child

contrast.india: Adrenaline usually given in hospital; autoinjectors uncommon and costly.
contrast.australia: PBS-subsidised autoinjectors carried by at-risk children; schools hold action plans and trained staff.

contrast.india: Antihistamine and hydrocortisone often given first in practice.
contrast.australia: IM adrenaline first; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts only (ASCIA).

flashcards.front: IM adrenaline dose for paediatric anaphylaxis?
flashcards.back: 0.01 mg/kg (0.01 mL/kg of 1:1000), max 0.5 mg, anterolateral thigh.

flashcards.front: Which autoinjector for a 16 kg child?
flashcards.back: 150 microg (for 7.5-20 kg).

flashcards.front: Which autoinjector for a 25 kg child?
flashcards.back: 300 microg (for over 20 kg).

flashcards.front: Minimum observation after adrenaline for anaphylaxis (ASCIA)?
flashcards.back: At least 4 hours after the last dose.

flashcards.front: Biggest risk factor for fatal food anaphylaxis in children?
flashcards.back: Asthma, particularly if poorly controlled.

flashcards.back: Serum mast cell tryptase, taken within 1-2 hours of onset.

quiz.stem: A 5-year-old girl weighing 18 kg develops lip swelling, widespread hives and a hoarse voice 10 minutes after eating a biscuit containing cashew at a party. She is wheezy. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
options: Oral cetirizine
IV hydrocortisone
Salbutamol via spacer
Adrenaline 150 microg autoinjector into the lateral thigh
Adrenaline 300 microg autoinjector into the deltoid
quiz.explanation:
Hives and lip swelling plus a **hoarse voice and wheeze** after nut ingestion is **anaphylaxis** (skin features plus airway and respiratory involvement). First-line treatment is **IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh**, where absorption is fastest.

For children **7.5-20 kg** the autoinjector dose is **150 microg**; over 20 kg it is 300 microg. The weight-based dose (0.01 mg/kg = 0.18 mg) is close to 150 microg.

Salbutamol may be given **after** adrenaline for persistent wheeze. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts and do not treat airway oedema or shock.
whyWrong: Antihistamines do not treat airway oedema or shock and are too slow.
Steroids are adjuncts at best and act over hours.
Salbutamol is given after adrenaline, not instead of it.
Wrong dose for her weight, and the thigh is the recommended site.

quiz.stem: A 9-year-old boy with peanut allergy and asthma was given IM adrenaline by his teacher 40 minutes ago for vomiting, wheeze and throat tightness after eating a muesli bar. In the emergency department he is now comfortable, with a clear chest, BP 105/65 mmHg and no urticaria. His mother asks to take him home. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: He can go home now because his symptoms have resolved
He should be observed for at least 4 hours after the adrenaline dose before discharge
He can go home if he takes an oral antihistamine for 3 days
He needs admission for 48 hours of IV corticosteroids
He should go home and see an allergist within a week, without an autoinjector until then
quiz.explanation:
Adrenaline wears off within minutes to an hour, and **biphasic reactions** can occur hours later. ASCIA recommends observation for **at least 4 hours after the last adrenaline dose**, and longer (often overnight) for a severe reaction, more than one dose needed, **asthma**, or late presentation. This boy has asthma, which is the strongest risk factor for fatal food anaphylaxis, so a longer observation period is reasonable.

Before discharge: an adrenaline autoinjector prescription and training, an ASCIA action plan (with a copy for school), asthma review and allergist referral.
whyWrong: Too early: biphasic reactions and waning adrenaline make immediate discharge unsafe.
Antihistamines do not prevent biphasic anaphylaxis.
Prolonged steroid admission is not indicated.
He must leave with an autoinjector and action plan.
quiz.ausPearl: ASCIA action plans are the standard document for schools and childcare in Australia.

quiz.stem: A 14-month-old boy (10 kg) is brought to the emergency department 15 minutes after his first taste of scrambled egg. He vomited twice and is now pale, floppy and unusually quiet. There is no rash. HR 175/min, capillary refill 4 seconds, BP 62/35 mmHg. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Give promethazine IM
Give IM adrenaline 0.1 mg into the anterolateral thigh
Give a 20 mL/kg fluid bolus and observe the response before any drug
Give ondansetron and reassess after an hour
Give IV adrenaline 1 mg
quiz.explanation:
Anaphylaxis can occur **without skin signs**. In young children, being **pale and floppy** after a likely allergen is a sign of cardiovascular involvement, and this infant is hypotensive and poorly perfused. The first treatment is **IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg** (0.1 mg = 0.1 mL of 1:1000 for 10 kg) into the lateral thigh, lying the child flat.

A fluid bolus (20 mL/kg) is appropriate **as well**, once access is obtained, but must not delay adrenaline. Promethazine is contraindicated in young children and worsens hypotension. IV adrenaline 1 mg is the adult cardiac arrest dose.
whyWrong: Sedating antihistamines are contraindicated in young children and worsen hypotension.
Fluids help but adrenaline comes first; delaying it is dangerous.
Treating vomiting misses anaphylactic shock.
A 1 mg IV bolus is an adult arrest dose and would be dangerous here.

lessons.title: Seizures and status epilepticus
objectives: Treat convulsive status epilepticus using the time-based RCH approach with midazolam first line
Identify simple and complex febrile seizures and counsel parents accurately
Find and treat reversible causes (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, meningitis, head injury)
Distinguish seizures from common mimics such as breath-holding spells and reflex anoxic syncope

sections.heading: Why timing matters
sections.body:
Most seizures stop by themselves within 5 minutes. A seizure lasting **5 minutes or more is unlikely to stop spontaneously**, and the longer it goes on the harder it is to terminate, because GABA-A receptors are internalised from the synapse (so benzodiazepines lose effect) while excitatory NMDA receptors increase. That is the mechanistic reason for **treating at 5 minutes** and escalating quickly.

**Convulsive status epilepticus** is now defined practically as a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without return to baseline in between. It carries risk of hypoxia, aspiration, hyperthermia and neuronal injury.

Common causes in children: **febrile status**, known epilepsy (missed medication), CNS infection, **hypoglycaemia**, electrolyte disturbance (hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia in infants), head injury (including abusive head trauma) and poisoning.

sections.heading: Status epilepticus: the RCH pathway
sections.body:
**0 minutes**: ABC, high-flow oxygen, recovery position, time the seizure. **Check glucose** (treat hypoglycaemia with 10% glucose 2 mL/kg).

**At 5 minutes: first-line benzodiazepine**

| Route | Midazolam dose |
|---|---|
| Buccal or intranasal | **0.3 mg/kg** (max 10 mg) |
| IM | 0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg) |
| IV/IO | 0.15 mg/kg (max 5 mg) |

Midazolam by the buccal or intranasal route is ideal pre-hospital and for carers (it is on many children's seizure management plans). IV diazepam is an alternative when access exists. Rectal diazepam is used less now.

**At 10 minutes**: if still seizing, **one repeat dose** of benzodiazepine. Count doses already given by paramedics or parents; more than two doses causes respiratory depression without much extra benefit.

**At 15-20 minutes: second-line agent** (loading doses per RCH or local guideline):
- **Levetiracetam** IV, or
- **Phenytoin** IV (ECG monitoring; avoid in known phenytoin-sensitive epilepsy or suspected drug-induced seizures), or
- Phenobarbital (often preferred in neonates).

**Around 40 minutes (refractory)**: rapid sequence intubation with an anaesthetic agent, and PICU.

**Look for the cause** in parallel: glucose, electrolytes (sodium, calcium, magnesium), blood gas, FBC, cultures, anticonvulsant levels if relevant, toxicology. CT if focal features, head injury or no recovery. LP only when stable, with no raised ICP signs.

sections.heading: What to test, and when not to
sections.body:
Tailor investigations to the child, not to the fact of a seizure.

| Situation | Investigations |
|---|---|
| Any seizure with ongoing reduced consciousness | **Bedside glucose**, venous gas, electrolytes (sodium, calcium, magnesium), FBC, blood culture if febrile |
| Infant under 6 months, or no fever and first seizure | Glucose, sodium, calcium and magnesium are more likely to be abnormal; consider metabolic screen and septic workup |
| Suspected meningitis/encephalitis | Blood culture and antibiotics (plus aciclovir if encephalitis possible) first; LP only when stable with no raised ICP signs |
| Focal seizure, focal deficit, head injury, not recovering | **CT** urgently (MRI later for epilepsy workup) |
| Known epilepsy | Anticonvulsant levels where useful (for example phenytoin), and look for triggers such as missed doses or intercurrent illness |
| Possible ingestion | Toxicology advice, ECG (wide QRS with TCAs) |
| Unexplained seizure in an infant | Consider abusive head trauma: CT, ophthalmology, skeletal survey |

A **first unprovoked afebrile seizure** in a well child who has recovered is usually referred to a paediatrician for **EEG** (which helps classify the epilepsy syndrome and predict recurrence), with MRI if focal features. A single seizure is not epilepsy: epilepsy is usually diagnosed after two or more unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart. Those details are covered in the chronic conditions topic. Driving is not an issue for young children, but for adolescents Austroads fitness-to-drive standards apply after a seizure.

sections.heading: Febrile seizures
sections.body:
The commonest seizure of childhood: about **3% of children** have one, between **6 months and 6 years**, with fever and no CNS infection or metabolic cause.

| Simple | Complex |
|---|---|
| Generalised | Focal features |
| Under 15 minutes | 15 minutes or longer |
| Single in 24 hours | Recurs within 24 hours |
| Full recovery within about an hour | Prolonged post-ictal state or Todd paresis |

**Assessment**: find the source of fever. The key question is **"could this be meningitis?"** Look for meningism, bulging fontanelle, petechiae, prolonged drowsiness. Children under 12-18 months may not show meningism, so senior review and a lower threshold for LP apply in the very young, the unimmunised, or those pre-treated with antibiotics. Routine bloods, EEG and imaging are not needed after a simple febrile seizure.

**Counselling (what parents need to hear)**:
- It is frightening but a simple febrile seizure **does not cause brain damage**.
- About **1 in 3 children have another** febrile seizure; risk is higher if the first was under 18 months, there is a family history, or it occurred at a low temperature or soon after fever onset.
- The risk of later epilepsy is only slightly above the general population for simple seizures (higher for complex ones).
- **Paracetamol or ibuprofen do not prevent febrile seizures**; use them only for comfort.
- First aid: lie the child on the side, nothing in the mouth, time it, call an ambulance if it lasts 5 minutes or more.

sections.heading: Things that look like seizures
sections.body:
| Condition | Clues |
|---|---|
| **Cyanotic breath-holding spell** | 6-18 months onset; triggered by anger or frustration; cries, stops breathing in expiration, goes blue, may go limp or briefly stiffen; rapid recovery |
| **Reflex anoxic seizure (pallid spell)** | Triggered by sudden pain or fright (minor head bump); goes pale and limp from vagal asystole; may have brief jerks; rapid recovery |
| Vasovagal syncope | Older child, standing, warning (hot, dizzy, vision greying), brief |
| Rigors | Shaking with fever, conscious throughout |
| Infant reflux (Sandifer) | Arching and posturing after feeds |
| Benign sleep myoclonus | Jerks only in sleep, stop on waking |

Breath-holding is associated with **iron deficiency**; checking iron studies and treating deficiency reduces spells. The key discriminator from epilepsy is the **trigger** preceding the event.

sections.heading: Traps
sections.body:
- The answer to "child still seizing at 5 minutes, no IV access" is **buccal or intranasal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg** (or IM).
- Always check the glucose. An AMC stem that gives a BSL of 2.1 mmol/L wants 10% glucose, not more midazolam.
- Maximum two benzodiazepine doses in total, including pre-hospital doses; the next step is a second-line agent.
- Simple febrile seizure in a well child with an obvious source (otitis media, viral URTI) and full recovery: no LP, no EEG, no imaging, reassure and educate.
- A seizing infant with no fever and a retinal haemorrhage or unexplained bruise: think abusive head trauma.
- Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures: parents often ask.

keyPoints: Treat seizures lasting 5 minutes or more.
Midazolam first line: 0.3 mg/kg buccal/intranasal, 0.2 mg/kg IM, 0.15 mg/kg IV.
Maximum two benzodiazepine doses, then levetiracetam or phenytoin.
Always check glucose: 10% glucose 2 mL/kg for hypoglycaemia.
Febrile seizures: 6 months to 6 years, about 3% of children, recurrence about 1 in 3.
Simple febrile seizure needs no EEG, imaging or routine bloods; exclude meningitis clinically.
Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures.
redFlags: Seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer
Not returning to baseline after the seizure
Meningism, petechial rash or bulging fontanelle
Focal neurological signs
Hypoglycaemia or hyponatraemia
Seizure in an infant with unexplained injury

contrast.australia: Buccal or intranasal midazolam is preferred and appears on many children's seizure management plans.
Levetiracetam or phenytoin per RCH CPG; levetiracetam increasingly first choice.
