flashcards.back: 0.3 mg/kg (max 10 mg).

flashcards.front: IM midazolam dose for a seizing child?
flashcards.back: 0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg).

flashcards.front: When do you give the first benzodiazepine in a convulsing child?
flashcards.back: When the seizure has lasted 5 minutes.

flashcards.front: Recurrence risk after a first febrile seizure?
flashcards.back: About 1 in 3.

flashcards.front: Age range for febrile seizures?
flashcards.back: 6 months to 6 years.

flashcards.front: Investigation that may reduce cyanotic breath-holding spells?
flashcards.back: Iron studies: treating iron deficiency reduces spells.

quiz.stem: A 3-year-old boy (15 kg) with known epilepsy has been having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure for 7 minutes when paramedics arrive at his home. No medication has been given. They are unable to obtain IV access. Blood glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
options: IV phenytoin 20 mg/kg
Rectal paracetamol
Intranasal or buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg
Oral levetiracetam
Wait until 15 minutes before giving medication
quiz.explanation:
A seizure lasting **5 minutes or more** needs treatment because it is unlikely to stop on its own and becomes harder to terminate with time. The first-line drug is a **benzodiazepine**, and without IV access **buccal or intranasal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg** (max 10 mg) or IM midazolam 0.2 mg/kg is used. For 15 kg that is 4.5 mg.

If he is still seizing 5 minutes later, one further benzodiazepine dose may be given; then a second-line agent (levetiracetam or phenytoin) IV/IO.

Glucose has been checked and is normal, which is the right habit.
whyWrong: Phenytoin is second-line and needs IV/IO access.
Paracetamol does not stop seizures.
Oral medication is unsafe and ineffective in a convulsing child.
Delaying treatment beyond 5 minutes makes the seizure harder to stop.

quiz.stem: A 20-month-old girl had a 2-minute generalised seizure at home while febrile with a runny nose. On arrival 90 minutes later she is alert, playing and drinking. Temperature 38.9 °C, no rash, no neck stiffness, fontanelle closed, left tympanic membrane red and bulging. She is fully immunised. Her parents ask what this means. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Lumbar puncture to exclude meningitis
Arrange an EEG and CT brain
Start regular paracetamol to prevent further seizures
Treat the otitis media as appropriate, explain that about 1 in 3 children have another febrile seizure, and teach seizure first aid
Start oral sodium valproate
quiz.explanation:
This is a **simple febrile seizure**: generalised, under 15 minutes, single, full recovery, in a well, immunised child aged 6 months to 6 years with an identified source. No EEG, imaging or LP is needed when there are no features of meningitis.

Management is to **treat the source**, reassure and educate: febrile seizures do not cause brain damage, **recurrence occurs in about a third**, epilepsy risk is only slightly raised, and **antipyretics do not prevent recurrences**. Teach first aid (side position, nothing in the mouth, call an ambulance at 5 minutes).

Anticonvulsants are not used for simple febrile seizures.
whyWrong: LP is not needed in a well, immunised child with no meningism and a clear source.
EEG and imaging add nothing after a simple febrile seizure.
Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures.
Long-term anticonvulsants are not indicated for simple febrile seizures.

quiz.stem: A 13-month-old boy is brought in after two episodes this week. Each time he was told 'no', he cried vigorously, then went silent, turned blue around the lips, went limp for about 15 seconds with a few jerks, and then recovered fully within a minute. Development and examination are normal. What is the most useful investigation?
options: EEG
MRI brain
Iron studies and full blood count
24-hour Holter monitor
Serum calcium and magnesium
quiz.explanation:
The **trigger** (frustration, being told off) followed by **crying, breath-holding in expiration, cyanosis, brief limpness and quick recovery** is a **cyanotic breath-holding spell**, common between 6 and 18 months. Brief jerks can occur from cerebral hypoxia and do not indicate epilepsy.

Breath-holding spells are associated with **iron deficiency anaemia**, and iron supplementation reduces their frequency even when haemoglobin is only mildly low. So FBC and iron studies are the most useful tests. Reassurance, and advice not to reinforce the behaviour, are the mainstay.

An ECG is reasonable if pallid spells are frequent or atypical (to exclude long QT), but EEG and MRI are not indicated.
whyWrong: EEG is not needed when the event is clearly provoked with rapid recovery.
Imaging is not indicated with normal development and examination.
Cardiac monitoring is for atypical or pallid spells, not classic cyanotic spells.
Hypocalcaemic seizures are not triggered by crying and are not typical at this age.

lessons.title: Dehydration, fluids and paediatric DKA
objectives: Estimate dehydration using the most reliable signs (capillary refill, skin turgor, breathing pattern)
Choose oral, nasogastric or IV rehydration and calculate maintenance fluids
Diagnose and grade paediatric DKA and explain why fluids are replaced more slowly than in adults
Recognise and treat cerebral oedema in DKA

sections.heading: Why fluid in children is its own subject
sections.body:
Children have a higher proportion of body water, a higher metabolic rate and a larger surface area to volume ratio than adults, so they dehydrate faster. Infants also depend on others for drinks. **Gastroenteritis** (now far less often rotavirus in Australia thanks to the vaccine) is the usual cause, and **DKA** is both the most common way type 1 diabetes presents in young children and the leading cause of diabetes-related death in childhood.

The mechanistic thread in this lesson is **sodium and water across the blood-brain barrier**. Hypotonic fluids and rapid falls in osmolality let water move into brain cells, causing **hyponatraemic encephalopathy** or **cerebral oedema**. That is why Australian paediatric guidance uses isotonic fluids and, in DKA, replaces deficit slowly.

sections.heading: Assessing dehydration
sections.body:
Weight loss from a recent known weight is the gold standard but rarely available. Of the clinical signs, the **most useful individually** are:

- **Prolonged capillary refill** (over 2 seconds, centrally)
- **Reduced skin turgor**
- **Abnormal respiratory pattern** (deep, acidotic breathing)

RCH groups dehydration as:

| Degree | Signs |
|---|---|
| **Mild (under 4%)** | No signs |
| **Moderate (4-6%)** | Delayed capillary refill, increased respiratory rate, mildly reduced turgor, dry mucosa, sunken eyes |
| **Severe (7% or more)** | Very delayed capillary refill, mottled skin, deep breathing, lethargy, **signs of shock** |

Red flags in a child with vomiting/diarrhoea that suggest something other than simple gastro: **bilious (green) vomiting** (malrotation, obstruction), blood in stool, severe abdominal pain, high fever or toxicity, age under 6 months, headache and drowsiness, and **polyuria despite dehydration** (diabetes). Always consider DKA in a "dehydrated" child with deep breathing and no diarrhoea.

sections.heading: Rehydration and maintenance fluids
sections.body:
**Oral first**. Mild and moderate dehydration are treated with **oral rehydration solution** (for example Gastrolyte or Hydralyte) given as small frequent volumes (5 mL every few minutes in a vomiting toddler). Continue breastfeeding. Avoid undiluted fruit juice and soft drinks (high sugar, low sodium, worsen diarrhoea).

**Ondansetron**: a single oral dose for children over 6 months with vomiting improves the success of oral rehydration (RCH).

**Nasogastric rehydration** is preferred over IV for moderate dehydration when oral fails. RCH describes **rapid NG rehydration of 25 mL/kg/h for 4 hours** (100 mL/kg total) in suitable children.

**IV fluids** for severe dehydration, shock, or failed NG:
- Shock: **10-20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus**, reassess, repeat.
- Then replace deficit plus maintenance using **isotonic fluid with glucose** (for example 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose, or Plasma-Lyte 148 with 5% glucose). Check electrolytes and glucose.

**Maintenance fluid (Holliday-Segar, "4-2-1")**

| Weight | Per hour |
|---|---|
| First 10 kg | 4 mL/kg/h |
| Next 10 kg | 2 mL/kg/h |
| Each kg over 20 | 1 mL/kg/h |

Example: 25 kg = 40 + 20 + 5 = **65 mL/h**. Deficit (mL) = % dehydration x weight (kg) x 10.

Antidiarrhoeal drugs (loperamide) are contraindicated in young children. Antibiotics are not routine.

sections.heading: Paediatric DKA: mechanism
sections.body:
Absolute insulin deficiency means cells cannot use glucose. Counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol, catecholamines) drive **gluconeogenesis and lipolysis**; free fatty acids become **ketones** (beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate), causing a **high anion gap metabolic acidosis**. Hyperglycaemia causes **osmotic diuresis**, with loss of water, sodium and potassium. Total body potassium is depleted even when the serum level looks normal or high, because acidosis and insulin lack shift potassium out of cells.

**Diagnosis** (ISPAD/RCH): **hyperglycaemia (glucose over 11 mmol/L)**, **venous pH under 7.3 or low bicarbonate** (the bicarbonate threshold differs slightly between guideline versions: check RCH/ISPAD), and **ketonaemia** (blood beta-hydroxybutyrate 3 mmol/L or more) or ketonuria.

**Severity by pH**: mild 7.2-7.3, moderate 7.1-7.2, **severe under 7.1**.

Presentation: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, bedwetting in a previously dry child, abdominal pain, vomiting, **Kussmaul breathing**, ketotic breath, drowsiness. Young children are often misdiagnosed with gastroenteritis or a chest infection (deep breathing mistaken for respiratory distress).

sections.heading: Treating DKA and recognising cerebral oedema
sections.body:
Principles (follow the RCH/state DKA protocol; seek paediatric endocrinology/PICU advice):

1. **Resuscitation**: ABC. If shocked or poorly perfused, **bolus 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride** (repeat if needed). Avoid large, repeated boluses in a child who is not shocked.
2. **Deficit replacement slowly, over about 48 hours**, plus maintenance, using isotonic fluid. This is much slower than adult protocols.
3. **Insulin infusion 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h**, started **after fluids have been running for about 1-2 hours**. **No insulin bolus.**
4. **Potassium**: add to fluids once serum potassium is known and the child is passing urine (unless hyperkalaemic). Insulin drives potassium into cells and can cause dangerous hypokalaemia.
5. **Add glucose** to fluids when blood glucose falls to around 14-15 mmol/L, so insulin can continue until ketones clear. Aim for a slow fall in glucose.
6. **No bicarbonate** (associated with cerebral oedema).
7. Hourly glucose, neuro obs and fluid balance; 2-4-hourly gas and electrolytes. The corrected sodium should rise as glucose falls; a falling sodium is a warning sign.

**Cerebral oedema** usually appears **4-12 hours after treatment starts**. Risk factors: **young age, new diagnosis, severe acidosis, high urea, low pCO2, bicarbonate use, rapid fluid administration**, and failure of sodium to rise.

Warning signs: **headache, irritability, falling GCS, bradycardia with rising BP (Cushing response)**, vomiting recurring after initial improvement, incontinence, cranial nerve palsy, abnormal posturing.

Treatment: do not wait for imaging. Elevate the head, **reduce fluid rate**, give **mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg or 3% hypertonic saline** (per protocol), call PICU, then CT once stabilised.

sections.heading: How the AMC tests this
sections.body:
- The three most useful dehydration signs: **capillary refill, skin turgor, respiratory pattern**.
- Moderate dehydration with vomiting: **ORS plus single-dose ondansetron**, then NG if failing. IV is not first choice.
- Bilious vomiting is never "just gastro".
- A child with polyuria, weight loss and new bedwetting needs a **same-day finger-prick glucose and ketones**, not a urine culture next week.
- In paediatric DKA, the wrong answers include: insulin bolus, starting insulin before fluids, bicarbonate, and adult-style rapid litres of saline.
- **Headache and bradycardia during DKA treatment = cerebral oedema**: mannitol or hypertonic saline immediately.

keyPoints: Best dehydration signs: prolonged capillary refill, reduced skin turgor, abnormal respiratory pattern.
Oral rehydration solution first; single-dose ondansetron over 6 months; NG before IV.
Maintenance 4-2-1 mL/kg/h with isotonic fluid plus glucose.
DKA: glucose over 11, venous pH under 7.3 or low bicarbonate, ketones 3 mmol/L or more.
Paediatric DKA: deficit over about 48 hours, insulin 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h after 1-2 hours of fluids, no bolus.
Add potassium early and glucose when BSL falls to about 14-15 mmol/L; no bicarbonate.
Cerebral oedema: headache, falling GCS, bradycardia, hypertension; treat with mannitol or 3% saline.
redFlags: Bilious vomiting
Signs of shock (mottling, capillary refill over 3 s, lethargy)
Deep sighing breathing without diarrhoea (think DKA)
Headache or bradycardia during DKA treatment
Falling sodium during DKA treatment
Infant under 6 months with high-output diarrhoea

contrast.india: Hypotonic fluids (for example N/5 or N/2 with dextrose) historically common.
contrast.australia: Isotonic fluid with glucose (0.9% saline + 5% glucose or Plasma-Lyte + glucose) to avoid hyponatraemia.

contrast.india: IV fluids are often started early.
contrast.australia: ORS, ondansetron and rapid nasogastric rehydration preferred before IV (RCH).

contrast.india: DKA at presentation is common, often after missed diagnosis.
contrast.australia: Also common; public campaigns (e.g. the 4Ts: toilet, thirsty, tired, thinner) promote same-day glucose testing.

flashcards.front: Three most useful clinical signs of dehydration in children?
flashcards.back: Prolonged capillary refill, reduced skin turgor, abnormal (deep) respiratory pattern.

flashcards.front: Hourly maintenance fluid for a 25 kg child?
Insulin infusion rate in paediatric DKA?
flashcards.back: 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h, started after 1-2 hours of fluids; no bolus.

flashcards.front: Over what period is the fluid deficit replaced in paediatric DKA?
flashcards.back: About 48 hours.

flashcards.front: Classic signs of cerebral oedema in DKA?
flashcards.back: Headache, irritability, falling GCS, bradycardia, rising BP.

flashcards.front: Drug treatment for cerebral oedema in DKA?
flashcards.back: Mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg or 3% hypertonic saline, plus head elevation and fluid restriction.

quiz.stem: A 2-year-old boy has had vomiting and watery diarrhoea for 2 days. He has vomited small sips of water. He is alert but irritable, with dry lips, sunken eyes, capillary refill of 3 seconds and mildly reduced skin turgor. HR 140/min. No blood in the stool and no bilious vomiting. What is the most appropriate management?
options: A single oral dose of ondansetron, then small frequent volumes of oral rehydration solution
IV 0.45% sodium chloride with 5% glucose at maintenance
Oral loperamide and lemonade
Admit for IV antibiotics
Nil by mouth for 12 hours to rest the gut
quiz.explanation:
He has **moderate dehydration (about 4-6%)**: prolonged capillary refill, reduced turgor, dry mucosa and tachycardia, but no shock.

First-line treatment is **oral rehydration solution** in small, frequent volumes. A **single dose of oral ondansetron** (children over 6 months) reduces vomiting and makes oral rehydration more likely to succeed. If oral intake fails, **nasogastric rehydration** is preferred to IV.

IV fluids are for shock, severe dehydration or NG failure, and hypotonic fluids like 0.45% saline increase hyponatraemia risk. Loperamide is contraindicated in young children, and fizzy drinks have too little sodium and too much sugar.
whyWrong: IV is not first-line for moderate dehydration, and hypotonic fluid risks hyponatraemia.
Loperamide is contraindicated in young children; soft drinks worsen diarrhoea.
Antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis.
Fasting worsens dehydration.

quiz.stem: An 8-year-old girl is diagnosed with new-onset DKA. Weight 25 kg. Venous pH 7.05, bicarbonate 5 mmol/L, glucose 32 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, blood ketones 6.2 mmol/L. She is alert with capillary refill of 2 seconds and normal BP. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
options: IV insulin bolus 0.1 units/kg, then infusion
IV sodium bicarbonate to correct pH
1 litre of 0.9% sodium chloride over 1 hour, then insulin
Isotonic fluid to replace the deficit slowly over about 48 hours plus maintenance, with insulin infusion 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h starting after 1-2 hours and potassium added once she passes urine
Subcutaneous insulin and oral fluids on the ward
quiz.explanation:
This is **severe DKA** (pH under 7.1). She is not shocked, so there is no need for large boluses. Paediatric DKA management differs from adults because of the risk of **cerebral oedema**:

- Replace the **deficit slowly over about 48 hours** plus maintenance, with isotonic fluid.
- Start **insulin infusion 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h** after fluids have been running for 1-2 hours; **no bolus**.
- Add **potassium** once the level is known and she is passing urine, because insulin will drive potassium into cells.
- **No bicarbonate.**
- Add glucose when BSL falls to about 14-15 mmol/L, and monitor neuro obs hourly.

She has several cerebral oedema risk factors: new diagnosis and severe acidosis.
whyWrong: Insulin boluses are avoided in paediatric DKA; they cause rapid osmolar shifts and hypokalaemia.
Bicarbonate is associated with cerebral oedema and is not given.
Adult-style rapid litres risk cerebral oedema in a child who is not shocked.
Severe DKA needs IV insulin and close monitoring, ideally HDU/PICU.

quiz.stem: A 5-year-old boy is 6 hours into treatment for newly diagnosed DKA. He was alert on arrival but now complains of a headache and has become irritable and confused. HR has fallen from 120/min to 62/min and BP has risen from 100/60 to 130/85 mmHg. Blood glucose is 12 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Arrange an urgent CT brain before any treatment
Give IV mannitol (or 3% hypertonic saline), elevate the head of the bed and reduce the IV fluid rate
Give a 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus
Increase the insulin infusion rate
Give IV atropine for the bradycardia
quiz.explanation:
Headache, irritability, falling conscious state, **bradycardia and rising blood pressure** a few hours into DKA treatment are the classic picture of **cerebral oedema**, the leading cause of death in paediatric DKA. It typically occurs 4-12 hours after treatment starts, and risk is higher in young children with new-onset diabetes.

Treat clinically **without waiting for imaging**: **mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg IV or 3% hypertonic saline**, head of the bed elevated, reduce fluid rate, and call PICU for airway support. CT is done once the child is stabilised, to exclude other pathology such as thrombosis or haemorrhage.
whyWrong: Imaging first delays life-saving treatment; this is a clinical diagnosis.
More fluid worsens cerebral oedema.
Faster insulin speeds the osmolar fall and is not the treatment.
The bradycardia is a Cushing response to raised ICP; atropine treats nothing.

quiz.stem: A 22 kg child with gastroenteritis is being admitted for IV fluids after failing oral and nasogastric rehydration. She is not shocked, and her electrolytes are normal. Which IV maintenance regimen is most appropriate before deficit is added?
options: 0.18% sodium chloride with 4% glucose at 62 mL/h
5% glucose alone at 62 mL/h
0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose at 62 mL/h
0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose at 88 mL/h
Plasma-Lyte 148 at 44 mL/h
quiz.explanation:
Using **Holliday-Segar (4-2-1)**: 4 mL/kg/h for the first 10 kg (40), 2 mL/kg/h for the next 10 kg (20), and 1 mL/kg/h for each kg above 20 (2) gives **62 mL/h**.

Australian paediatric guidance uses **isotonic fluid with glucose** (0.9% sodium chloride + 5% glucose, or Plasma-Lyte 148 + 5% glucose) for maintenance, because sick children secrete ADH and hypotonic fluids cause **hyponatraemia and encephalopathy**. Glucose is included to prevent hypoglycaemia and ketosis.

The deficit is then added on top, and electrolytes are rechecked within 24 hours (sooner if abnormal).
whyWrong: Hypotonic fluid risks hyponatraemic encephalopathy.
5% glucose alone is effectively free water and very dangerous.
88 mL/h is 4 mL/kg/h for all 22 kg, an overestimate.
Wrong rate and no glucose for a child who is not eating.

lessons.title: Acute abdomen and surgical emergencies
objectives: Recognise intussusception from its history and arrange ultrasound and air enema reduction
Treat bilious vomiting in an infant as malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise
Distinguish pyloric stenosis, appendicitis and testicular torsion in children
Know which findings mandate immediate surgical referral

sections.heading: The approach
sections.body:
Abdominal pain and vomiting are common in children and usually benign (constipation, gastroenteritis, mesenteric adenitis). The AMC wants you to pick out the surgical emergencies quickly, because each has a time window:

| Condition | Typical age | Time-critical because |
|---|---|---|
| **Malrotation with volvulus** | Neonate/infant | Midgut ischaemia within hours |
| **Intussusception** | 3 months-3 years (peak about 6-12 months) | Bowel ischaemia and perforation |
| **Pyloric stenosis** | 2-8 weeks | Dehydration and alkalosis (medical emergency first) |
| **Appendicitis** | Any; perforates more often under 5 | Perforation and peritonitis |
| **Testicular torsion** | Neonatal and adolescent peaks | Testis viability falls steeply after about 6 hours |
| **Incarcerated inguinal hernia** | Infants, especially preterm | Strangulation |

Always examine the **groin and genitals** in a child with abdominal pain or vomiting; boys often will not mention testicular pain.

sections.heading: Intussusception
sections.body:
**Pathogenesis**: a proximal segment of bowel telescopes into the distal segment, usually **ileocolic**. In infants the lead point is typically hypertrophied **Peyer patches** after a viral illness. In older children (over about 3 years) look for a **pathological lead point**: Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma, or bowel wall haematoma in **Henoch-Schonlein purpura** (IgA vasculitis). Venous and lymphatic obstruction causes mucosal oedema and bleeding, then arterial compromise.

A small increased risk has been observed in the weeks after rotavirus vaccination, which is why strict upper age limits apply to rotavirus doses.

**Clinical features**
- **Episodic, inconsolable crying** every 10-20 minutes with **pallor and drawing up of the legs**, settling in between
- Vomiting, becoming **bilious** later
- **Lethargy** between episodes (sometimes the dominant feature; can mimic sepsis or encephalopathy)
- Sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant, empty right iliac fossa
- **"Redcurrant jelly" stool** (blood and mucus) is a **late** sign: do not wait for it

**Investigations**: **ultrasound** is the test of choice (target or "doughnut" sign on transverse view, "pseudokidney" on longitudinal). Plain X-ray may show obstruction or free air but can be normal.

**Management**: resuscitate (IV fluids, NG if vomiting), involve surgeons, then **air (pneumatic) enema reduction** under radiological guidance, which succeeds in most cases. **Surgery** if there is **peritonitis, perforation or shock that doesn't respond**, or the enema fails. Recurrence is possible, so parents are told to return if symptoms recur.

sections.heading: Bilious vomiting, projectile vomiting and appendicitis
sections.body:
**Malrotation with midgut volvulus**. Incomplete rotation leaves a narrow mesenteric base and Ladd bands; the midgut twists on the superior mesenteric artery. **Bilious (green) vomiting in a neonate or infant is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.** The abdomen may be soft and flat early. Emergency **upper GI contrast study** (duodenojejunal flexure malpositioned, "corkscrew" duodenum) or immediate laparotomy if unstable. Treatment is **Ladd procedure**. Delay means loss of the midgut.

**Pyloric stenosis**. Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle; more common in **first-born boys**, age **2-8 weeks**. **Non-bilious projectile vomiting** after feeds, a hungry baby, weight loss, visible peristalsis, palpable "olive" in the epigastrium during a test feed. Bloods: **hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis** (loss of gastric HCl; the kidney retains sodium at the expense of potassium and hydrogen, giving paradoxical aciduria). Ultrasound confirms. **Correct fluids and electrolytes first** (it is a medical emergency before it is a surgical one), then pyloromyotomy.

**Appendicitis**. Periumbilical pain migrating to the RIF, anorexia, low-grade fever, pain with walking or hopping. Young children present atypically and **perforate more often**. Scores (Paediatric Appendicitis Score, Alvarado) help stratify. **Ultrasound** is the first imaging in children (avoid CT radiation where possible). Treatment is appendicectomy with antibiotics.

**Mesenteric adenitis**: follows a viral illness, high fever early, diffuse tenderness; a diagnosis of exclusion.

**Testicular torsion**: sudden severe scrotal pain, nausea, high-riding horizontal testis, **absent cremasteric reflex**. It is a **clinical diagnosis: urgent surgical exploration**; do not delay for ultrasound if suspicion is high. Torsion of a testicular appendage (hydatid of Morgagni) gives a "blue dot" and a preserved cremasteric reflex.

sections.heading: Common threads in management
sections.body:
- **Nil by mouth**, IV access, bloods (FBC, electrolytes, glucose, venous gas, group and hold), **fluid resuscitation** with isotonic crystalloid.
- **Nasogastric tube** on free drainage for bilious vomiting or obstruction.
- **Analgesia is appropriate and does not mask surgical signs.** IV morphine or intranasal fentanyl are commonly used in paediatric EDs.
- **Early paediatric surgical referral** for bilious vomiting, peritonism, suspected torsion or intussusception. In regional Australia this often means discussion with a tertiary paediatric surgical centre and retrieval.
- **Incarcerated inguinal hernia**: attempt gentle reduction with analgesia if no signs of strangulation, then early repair; all infant inguinal hernias need surgical repair (they do not close by themselves, unlike umbilical hernias, which usually do).
- Constipation is the commonest cause of acute abdominal pain in children presenting to GPs; but it is a diagnosis made after red flags are excluded.
- **Medical mimics of a surgical abdomen** to keep in mind: **DKA** (abdominal pain and vomiting with deep breathing: check glucose and ketones), **lower lobe pneumonia** (fever, tachypnoea, referred abdominal pain), **urinary tract infection**, **HSP** (purpuric rash on buttocks and legs, arthritis, colicky pain), streptococcal pharyngitis in school-age children, and in adolescent girls **ovarian torsion, ectopic pregnancy** (do a pregnancy test) and pelvic inflammatory disease.
- **Safety-netting** for children sent home with non-specific abdominal pain: return if pain becomes constant or localises to the right iliac fossa, green vomiting, blood in stool, fever, or the child becomes pale, floppy or unable to walk comfortably. Arrange review within 12-24 hours if uncertain.

sections.heading: Discriminating clues
sections.body:
- **Green vomit in a baby = surgical emergency** (malrotation). The next step is an urgent upper GI contrast study and surgical review, not "trial of reflux medication".
- **Episodic crying with pallor and legs drawn up, lethargic between episodes = intussusception**. Choose ultrasound, then air enema. Redcurrant jelly stool is late.
- Intussusception in a 6-year-old, or with purpuric rash on the legs: look for a lead point or HSP.
- **Projectile non-bilious vomiting at 5 weeks, hypochloraemic alkalosis** = pyloric stenosis; fix electrolytes before theatre.
- Suspected torsion: **explore within 6 hours**; ultrasound is the wrong answer if it would delay theatre.
- Always examine the testes in a boy with abdominal pain.

keyPoints: Bilious vomiting in an infant is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.
Intussusception: episodic inconsolable crying, drawing up legs, pallor, lethargy; redcurrant jelly stool is late.
Intussusception: ultrasound (target sign) then air enema; surgery if peritonitis or perforation.
Pyloric stenosis: 2-8 weeks, projectile non-bilious vomiting, hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; fix fluids first.
Young children perforate appendicitis more often; ultrasound is first-line imaging.
Testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis; explore urgently.
Analgesia does not mask surgical signs.
redFlags: Bilious (green) vomiting
Blood per rectum with abdominal pain
Peritonism or rigid abdomen
Sudden scrotal pain
Lethargy or pallor between bouts of crying
Irreducible groin lump

contrast.india: Hydrostatic (saline/barium) reduction or surgery depending on centre.
contrast.australia: Air (pneumatic) enema under fluoroscopy is standard in paediatric centres; surgery if it fails or peritonitis.

contrast.india: CT or clinical diagnosis depending on availability.
contrast.australia: Ultrasound first to limit radiation; regional sites often discuss with tertiary paediatric surgeons.

flashcards.front: Ultrasound sign of intussusception?
flashcards.back: Target or doughnut sign (transverse); pseudokidney (longitudinal).

flashcards.front: First-line treatment of uncomplicated intussusception?
flashcards.back: Air (pneumatic) enema reduction.

flashcards.front: Metabolic picture in pyloric stenosis?
flashcards.back: Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

flashcards.front: Bilious vomiting in a 2-week-old: what must be excluded?
flashcards.back: Malrotation with midgut volvulus (urgent upper GI contrast and surgical review).

flashcards.front: Cremasteric reflex in testicular torsion?
flashcards.back: Usually absent.

flashcards.front: Pathological lead point to consider in intussusception with purpura?
flashcards.back: Bowel wall haematoma from Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis).

quiz.stem: A 9-month-old boy has had episodes of screaming for 12 hours. Every 15 minutes he goes pale, draws his knees up and cries inconsolably for a few minutes, then lies quietly and seems unusually sleepy. He vomited twice. Temperature 37.4 °C, HR 150/min. A vague mass is felt in the right upper quadrant. The nappy contains normal stool. What is the most appropriate investigation?
options: Abdominal ultrasound
Stool culture
Urine microscopy and culture
CT abdomen with contrast
Barium swallow
quiz.explanation:
Episodic inconsolable crying with **pallor and drawing up of the legs**, **lethargy between episodes**, vomiting and a right upper quadrant mass in an infant is **intussusception**. The absence of redcurrant jelly stool does not exclude it: that is a late sign of mucosal ischaemia.

**Ultrasound** is the investigation of choice (target/doughnut sign), with high sensitivity and no radiation. If confirmed and there is no peritonitis or perforation, **air enema reduction** is the first-line treatment after resuscitation.
whyWrong: Stool culture is for infective diarrhoea and would delay diagnosis.
UTI is worth excluding in a febrile infant, but this picture is intussusception.
CT adds radiation and is unnecessary when ultrasound is diagnostic.
A barium swallow images the upper GI tract, not the ileocolic region.

quiz.stem: A 3-week-old girl, born at term, has had three episodes of green vomiting over the past 4 hours. She was feeding well until today. Her abdomen is soft and not distended. HR 170/min, capillary refill 2 seconds. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Change to a thickened formula and review in 48 hours
Start omeprazole for reflux
Nil by mouth, IV fluids, nasogastric tube and urgent paediatric surgical review with an upper GI contrast study
Pyloric ultrasound
Discharge with oral rehydration solution
quiz.explanation:
**Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise.** The abdomen is often soft and non-distended early, which falsely reassures. The midgut can become ischaemic within hours.

Management: **nil by mouth, IV access and fluids, NG tube on free drainage, urgent paediatric surgical review** and an emergency **upper GI contrast study** to look at the position of the duodenojejunal flexure. If the child is unstable, the surgeons will go straight to laparotomy (Ladd procedure).

Pyloric stenosis causes **non-bilious** vomiting because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla.
whyWrong: Treating as reflux can lose the entire midgut.
Reflux is never the explanation for bilious vomiting.
Pyloric stenosis gives non-bilious vomiting.
Discharge is unsafe for bilious vomiting in a neonate.

quiz.stem: A 5-week-old first-born boy has had increasingly forceful, non-bilious vomiting after every feed for a week. He is hungry immediately afterwards and has lost weight. He looks mildly dehydrated. Venous gas: pH 7.52, bicarbonate 34 mmol/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L, chloride 86 mmol/L. Ultrasound confirms a thickened, elongated pylorus. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Pyloromyotomy today
Oral rehydration solution and discharge
Start erythromycin
IV fluids with 0.9% sodium chloride and glucose plus potassium, and correct the alkalosis before surgery
Barium meal
quiz.explanation:
This is **pyloric stenosis**, with the classic **hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis** from loss of gastric acid. The kidney tries to preserve volume by retaining sodium in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions, worsening hypokalaemia and producing paradoxical aciduria.

It is a **medical emergency before it is a surgical one**. Operating on an alkalotic infant risks post-operative apnoea (alkalosis depresses respiratory drive) and arrhythmia. Rehydrate with **isotonic saline plus glucose, add potassium** once passing urine, and recheck electrolytes until chloride and bicarbonate normalise. **Pyloromyotomy** follows once corrected.
whyWrong: Surgery must wait until fluids and electrolytes are corrected.
He cannot keep oral fluids down and needs IV correction.
Erythromycin is associated with pyloric stenosis and is not a treatment.
The diagnosis is already confirmed on ultrasound.

lessons.title: Poisoning, button batteries and injuries
objectives: Risk-assess a childhood ingestion and use the Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26)
Manage button battery and magnet ingestion as time-critical emergencies
Decide when a child with a head injury needs CT using PECARN
Give burns first aid, estimate burn size in a child and know referral criteria

sections.heading: Unintentional injury and poisoning in Australian children
sections.body:
Injury is the leading cause of death in Australian children over 1 year. The big killers are **drowning** (toddlers), **transport injuries**, and falls; burns and poisoning cause a large share of hospital admissions. Toddlers (1-4 years) account for most accidental ingestions: they are mobile, curious and put everything in their mouths.

Two public health tools recur in AMC questions:
- The **Poisons Information Centre: 13 11 26**, available 24 hours nationally, for the public and clinicians.
- **Mandatory safety standards for button batteries** (introduced nationally in 2022: secure compartments, child-resistant packaging and warnings), after several Australian children died.

Always ask whether the story fits the child's development. **An injury or ingestion that does not match the history or the child's developmental stage raises concern for non-accidental injury** (see the child protection topic). A 4-month-old cannot roll off a change table onto a toy and fracture a femur by themselves, and cannot open a medicine bottle.

sections.heading: The poisoned child
sections.body:
**Risk assessment** is the core skill (as taught by Australian toxicology services): agent, dose (mg/kg), time since ingestion, clinical features, and patient factors (weight, comorbidities). Call **13 11 26** for advice.

Most ingestions in toddlers are non-toxic, but some agents **can kill a toddler with one or two tablets or a mouthful**:

- **Tricyclic antidepressants** (seizures, wide QRS arrhythmias)
- **Calcium channel blockers** (verapamil, diltiazem) and beta-blockers
- **Sulfonylureas** (delayed, prolonged hypoglycaemia)
- **Opioids** including methadone and buprenorphine (respiratory depression)
- **Clonidine** (bradycardia, hypotension, coma)
- **Eucalyptus oil** and other essential oils (CNS depression, aspiration pneumonitis): common in Australian homes
- **Button batteries**, multiple magnets, dishwasher and laundry detergent pods (caustic injury)
- Iron tablets, and paracetamol in large doses

**Paracetamol**: in an acute ingestion by a young child, assessment (serum paracetamol level at 4 hours or later) is usually needed if **200 mg/kg or more** has been taken (Australian and New Zealand consensus guidance). The level is plotted on the Australian nomogram (the treatment line starts at **150 mg/L at 4 hours**). Treatment is **acetylcysteine**, most effective within 8 hours.

**Decontamination**: activated charcoal is rarely used in children, only after toxicology advice, within about 1-2 hours of a significant ingestion of an adsorbable toxin, and only if the airway is protected. Never induce vomiting. Charcoal does not bind iron, lithium, alcohols or hydrocarbons.

**Observation periods** depend on the agent (for example, prolonged observation and serial glucose for sulfonylurea ingestion; ECG for TCAs).

**Prevention**: store medicines up high and locked, child-resistant packaging, never call medicine "lollies", return unused medicines to pharmacies (RUM project).

sections.heading: Button batteries, magnets and other foreign bodies
sections.body:
**Button batteries** (especially 20 mm lithium coin cells) lodged in the oesophagus generate an electrical current across the moist mucosa, producing **hydroxide ions and an alkaline caustic burn within 2 hours**. The burn can progress over days to perforation, tracheo-oesophageal fistula, or **aorto-oesophageal fistula with catastrophic haemorrhage**, sometimes weeks later.

- Suspected ingestion (witnessed, missing battery, or unexplained drooling, vomiting, food refusal, haematemesis or stridor in a toddler) needs an **urgent chest and abdominal X-ray** (neck to anus).
- On AP view a button battery shows a **"halo" or double-ring sign** and on lateral view a **step-off**, distinguishing it from a coin.
- **Oesophageal battery: endoscopic removal within 2 hours**, at a centre able to manage it, transferring immediately.
- While awaiting removal, some Australian and international guidance supports giving **honey** (in children over 1 year) or sucralfate within 12 hours of ingestion to coat the battery; follow Poisons Centre advice and do not delay transfer.
- A battery beyond the oesophagus in an asymptomatic child is usually managed with repeat X-ray to confirm passage, per local guidance.
- Follow-up for delayed complications is needed after removal.

**Multiple magnets** (or a magnet plus a metal object) can attract across bowel walls, causing pressure necrosis, perforation and fistulae: surgical review.

**Coins** in the oesophagus usually need removal if they do not pass; coins in the stomach usually pass.

sections.heading: Head injury and burns
sections.body:
**Head injury**. Most are minor. CT exposes children to ionising radiation (with a small lifetime cancer risk), so clinical decision rules identify who needs it. **PECARN** was the most accurate in the Australian and New Zealand PREDICT validation study.

- **High risk (CT recommended)**: GCS under 15 or other altered mental status, palpable or depressed skull fracture (under 2), or signs of basal skull fracture (2 and over: haemotympanum, Battle sign, raccoon eyes, CSF leak).
- **Intermediate risk** (observation vs CT, depending on number of features, clinician experience, worsening, parental preference): loss of consciousness, severe mechanism, vomiting or severe headache (2 and over); non-frontal scalp haematoma, LOC 5 seconds or more, severe mechanism, or not acting normally per parent (under 2).
- Others are low risk: discharge with written head injury advice.

Also consider: bleeding disorders or anticoagulants (lower threshold), and **abusive head trauma** in infants (no or trivial history, retinal haemorrhages, subdural haematomas of different ages).

**Burns**. Scalds from hot drinks and bath water are the commonest mechanism in toddlers.

- **First aid: cool running water for 20 minutes**, effective up to 3 hours after the burn. Remove jewellery and clothing (unless stuck). No ice, butter or toothpaste. Keep the child warm.
- **Size**: use the **Lund and Browder chart**, which adjusts for age (a young child's head is proportionally larger and legs smaller than an adult's). The child's palm plus fingers is about 1% TBSA. The adult "rule of nines" overestimates legs and underestimates the head in children. Erythema alone is not counted.
- **Depth**: superficial (red, painful, no blisters), partial thickness (blisters, painful, blanch), full thickness (white/leathery, painless).
- **IV fluid resuscitation** is needed in children with burns of about 10% TBSA or more, in addition to maintenance fluid.
- **Referral to a burns unit** (ANZBA criteria include): larger burns (roughly over 5% TBSA in a child), full thickness burns, burns to face, hands, feet, genitals, perineum or major joints, circumferential burns, electrical, chemical or inhalation injury, and **any suspicion of non-accidental injury** (for example sharply demarcated "glove and stocking" immersion burns with sparing of flexures, or cigarette burns).

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- Toddler with drooling and food refusal after a missing remote-control battery: **X-ray now**, then **remove within 2 hours** if oesophageal. Waiting for the battery to pass is wrong.
- "Who do you call?" **Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26.**
- A single adult tablet of a sulfonylurea, TCA, calcium channel blocker, clonidine or opioid can be lethal in a toddler: admit and observe, even if the child looks well.
- Paracetamol: 200 mg/kg or more acute ingestion in a young child needs a 4-hour level; treatment line starts at 150 mg/L at 4 hours.
- Head injury: know the PECARN high-risk features; a well child with a minor fall and no risk features goes home with advice.
- Burns: **20 minutes of cool running water**; Lund and Browder for children; think NAI with immersion patterns.
- Every injury: does the story fit the child's development?

keyPoints: Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26, 24 hours, nationally.
One pill can kill a toddler: TCAs, calcium channel blockers, sulfonylureas, opioids, clonidine; also eucalyptus oil.
Paracetamol: 200 mg/kg or more acute ingestion needs a 4-hour level; nomogram line starts at 150 mg/L; treat with acetylcysteine.
Button battery in the oesophagus: X-ray (halo sign) and endoscopic removal within 2 hours.
PECARN guides CT in paediatric head injury and performed best in Australian validation.
Burns: cool running water for 20 minutes, useful up to 3 hours; Lund and Browder chart for children.
Always ask whether the injury fits the history and development.

quiz.stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to a regional emergency department 40 minutes after her mother found her chewing a TV remote with the battery compartment open. One 20 mm coin-shaped battery is missing. She is drooling and refusing drinks. Chest X-ray shows a round radio-opaque object at the level of the thoracic inlet with a double-ring outline on the AP view. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Discharge and ask the parents to check her stools for the battery
Repeat the X-ray in 24 hours
Give activated charcoal
Induce vomiting with ipecac
Arrange immediate transfer for endoscopic removal within 2 hours of ingestion
quiz.explanation:
The **double-ring (halo) sign** identifies a **button battery**, and it is lodged in the **oesophagus**. The battery generates current in the moist mucosa, producing hydroxide and a **caustic burn within 2 hours**, which can progress to perforation or aorto-oesophageal fistula even after removal.

This is a time-critical emergency: **endoscopic removal within 2 hours**, arranging urgent transfer to a centre that can do it. Honey (over 1 year) may be given en route under Poisons Centre advice, but must not delay transfer. Charcoal does not bind batteries, and induced vomiting risks further injury and aspiration.
whyWrong: An oesophageal battery will not safely pass and causes burns within hours.
Waiting allows a full-thickness oesophageal burn to develop.
Charcoal does not adsorb batteries and would obscure endoscopy.
Induced vomiting is never recommended and risks aspiration.
quiz.ausPearl: Australia introduced mandatory safety standards for button batteries in 2022 after child deaths.

quiz.stem: A 20-month-old boy (12 kg) was found with his grandmother's pill organiser 30 minutes ago. One gliclazide tablet may be missing. He is well, playing, with a blood glucose of 5.4 mmol/L. His mother wants to take him home. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Discharge with advice to return if drowsy
Admit for prolonged observation with regular blood glucose monitoring, after discussion with the Poisons Information Centre
Give oral glucose and discharge after 1 hour
Give prophylactic IV octreotide and discharge
Gastric lavage
quiz.explanation:
**Sulfonylureas** such as gliclazide are among the drugs where **one tablet can cause severe hypoglycaemia in a toddler**. Onset can be **delayed** (several hours) and prolonged, especially with modified-release formulations, so a normal glucose now is not reassuring.

The child should be **admitted for prolonged observation** (commonly overnight, per toxicology advice) with regular glucose checks and access to food. Hypoglycaemia is treated with glucose, and **octreotide** is given if it recurs, not prophylactically. Call the **Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26)** for agent-specific advice.
whyWrong: Hypoglycaemia may be delayed; discharge is unsafe.
Prophylactic glucose can stimulate insulin release and mask delayed hypoglycaemia.
Octreotide is for established or recurrent hypoglycaemia, not prophylaxis.
Gastric lavage is not used in children for this ingestion.

quiz.stem: A 3-year-old boy pulled a cup of freshly made tea onto his chest 10 minutes ago. His father has brought him straight to a GP clinic next door. There is a red, blistering area over the front of the chest roughly the size of three of the child's palms. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Apply cool running water to the burn for 20 minutes
Apply ice packs
Apply silver sulfadiazine cream and dress
Pop the blisters and apply a dry dressing
Give a 20 mL/kg IV fluid bolus
quiz.explanation:
The first and most important step in any burn is **cool running water for 20 minutes**, which reduces tissue damage and pain and remains beneficial **up to 3 hours** after the injury. Remove clothing and jewellery unless stuck, and keep the rest of the child warm to avoid hypothermia.

This burn is about **3% TBSA** (the child's palm and fingers is about 1%) and partial thickness (blistered), so IV fluids are not needed (they are considered from about 10% TBSA). Ice causes vasoconstriction and further injury. Creams go on only after cooling and assessment, and chest burns in a toddler are usually discussed with a burns service. Also check the story fits.
whyWrong: Ice causes vasoconstriction, deepening the burn, and risks hypothermia.
Creams are not first aid; cooling comes first.
Blisters should not be deroofed as first aid.
A 3% partial thickness burn does not need IV resuscitation.
quiz.ausPearl: Australian burns first aid (ANZBA): cool running water for 20 minutes, up to 3 hours after the burn.

quiz.stem: A 6-year-old girl fell about 1 metre from monkey bars at school onto grass 2 hours ago. She cried immediately, did not lose consciousness, and has not vomited. She has a mild headache. GCS 15, she is acting normally, and there is no scalp haematoma, no signs of basal skull fracture and a normal neurological examination. What is the most appropriate management?
options: CT brain
Skull X-ray
Admit for 24 hours of neurological observations
Discharge with written head injury advice and clear instructions on when to return
MRI brain within a week
quiz.explanation:
Using **PECARN** for a child aged 2 or older, high-risk features are GCS under 15, altered mental status or signs of basal skull fracture; intermediate features include loss of consciousness, vomiting, severe headache or a severe mechanism (for example falls over 1.5 m in this age group). This girl has **no risk features** (a mild headache is not severe), so the risk of clinically important brain injury is very low and **CT is not indicated**.

She can be discharged with **written head injury advice**: return for worsening headache, repeated vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, seizure or weakness. PECARN performed best among decision rules in the Australian and New Zealand PREDICT study.
whyWrong: CT exposes her to radiation without benefit when she is very low risk.
Skull X-rays are not used to assess paediatric head injury.
Admission is not needed without risk features.
MRI has no role in routine minor head injury.
